items.hint1: Think about what kind of poem an epic is: how long it is, and who stands at its centre.
items.hint2: An epic is a long story-poem built around one great figure and the mighty deeds he performs. A theme is the main idea running through the whole work, not one event in it.
items.hint3: Cowardice is the opposite of what an epic praises, and sorrow is only a passing mood. Of the two left, which is the idea behind the whole poem, and which is only a result that may or may not come?
items.solution:
Answer: B. heroism

An epic is a long narrative poem that tells of the great deeds of a hero, often a figure of national or legendary importance, such as Sundiata or Achilles. Because the poem exists to celebrate those deeds, heroism is its dominant theme.

How to tell: ask what the whole poem is about from start to finish. In an epic, the battles, journeys and trials are there mainly to show the hero's courage and strength.

Why not the others:
A. cowardice: it is the opposite of what an epic praises; a coward may appear, but mainly to make the hero look greater.
C. sorrow: there may be sad episodes, such as a death, but sorrow is a passing mood, not the main idea.
D. victory: it is the outcome of some episodes, and epic heroes do not win every battle, so it is not the idea that runs through the whole poem.

Exam tip: when asked for the dominant theme of a type of poem, go back to its definition. Epic: a hero's deeds, so heroism. Elegy: death and loss, so mourning.

items.hint1: Read the sentence slowly and look for a word that appears more than once. Does it mean the same thing each time?
items.hint2: Some word play uses one word with two different meanings to make a joke. That is different from a device that reverses word order, or one that repeats sounds at the ends of lines.
items.hint3: Rhyme and chiasmus do not fit here. Decide between the device built on one word with two meanings and the device where one verb is joined to two objects in different senses. Which does this sentence show?
items.solution:
Answer: B. pun

A pun is a play on words that uses a word with two meanings, or two words that sound alike, to make a joke or a clever point. The humour comes from the reader noticing both meanings.

How to tell: 'mouse' appears twice. The first mouse is the small animal the cat hunts. The second, 'my mouse', is the computer mouse on the desk. The sentence is funny because the cat steps on the wrong kind of mouse.

Why not the others:
A. chiasmus: it reverses the order of words in two balanced parts, as in 'Fair is foul, and foul is fair'; nothing is reversed here.
C. rhyme: it is the matching of end sounds, usually at the ends of lines; the sentence has no rhyming pattern.
D. zeugma: one word, usually a verb, is joined to two objects in different senses, as in 'She lost her keys and her temper'; here no single verb does that double work.

Exam tip: if one word carries two different meanings in the same sentence, think pun. If one verb is stretched over two objects in different ways, think zeugma.

items.hint1: The question asks about attitude, meaning how the speaker feels about what they describe. Think of the literary term that names the feeling in a voice.
items.hint2: Plot is what happens, and setting is where and when it happens. Neither of these tells you how the speaker feels.
items.hint3: Of the two terms left, one is about the beat and flow of lines, and one is about the attitude you hear in the words. Which is which?
items.solution:
Answer: D. tone

Tone is the speaker's or writer's attitude towards the subject, such as serious, angry, playful or sad. We work it out from the words the writer chooses and the way they are put together.

How to tell: attitude is a feeling in the voice. Of the four terms, the one that names the feeling in the voice is tone. We say 'the tone is bitter' or 'the tone is gentle'.

Why not the others:
A. plot: it is the chain of events in a story, not the speaker's feeling about them.
B. rhythm: it is the beat or flow of the lines, which can support a tone but does not name the attitude.
C. setting: it is the time and place of the action.

Exam tip: the attitude of the speaker or writer is tone; the feeling created in the reader is mood. Exams often put the two side by side, so keep them apart.

items.hint1: The sounds of English fall into two groups: vowel sounds (a, e, i, o, u) and consonant sounds. The question is about one of these groups.
items.hint2: Alliteration repeats consonant sounds, usually at the start of nearby words. Onomatopoeia uses words that sound like what they name.
items.hint3: A pun plays on meaning rather than on sound. Test the option left over on 'the light of the fire is high': which sound keeps coming back, a vowel or a consonant?
items.solution:
Answer: B. assonance

Assonance is the repetition of the same vowel sound in words close together, as in 'the light of the fire is high', where the long 'i' sound comes back again and again. Poets use it to give lines a musical, flowing effect.

How to tell: the stem says vowel sounds. Of the sound devices offered, assonance is the one defined by repeated vowels.

Why not the others:
A. alliteration: it repeats consonant sounds, usually at the start of nearby words, as in 'big brown bear'.
C. onomatopoeia: it uses words that imitate the sound they name, such as 'buzz' or 'bang'.
D. pun: it plays on a word with two meanings, not on repeated sounds.

Exam tip: assonance is repeated vowels, alliteration is repeated consonants at the start of words, and consonance is repeated consonants inside or at the end of words. Learn the three together, because they are set as distractors for each other.

items.hint1: Picture a stage with a curtain across it. The question asks for the name of the part of the stage between the curtain and the audience.
items.hint2: Backstage is hidden behind the scenery, where actors wait and props are kept. The balcony is a raised seating area for the audience, not part of the stage.
items.hint3: Centre stage is the middle of the acting area, which is hidden when the curtain is closed. Which remaining term names the front part of the stage, framed by a large arch, that stays in view even when the curtain is down?
items.solution:
Answer: D. proscenium

In a traditional theatre the stage is framed by a large arch, the proscenium arch, with the main curtain hanging behind it. In the syllabus, the proscenium is taken as the front part of the stage, the part in front of the curtain and nearest the audience. The strip that sticks out beyond the arch is also called the apron.

How to tell: backstage, centre stage and the balcony each have their own place, and none of them is the stage area in front of the curtain. Of the four, the proscenium is the term for that front area.

Why not the others:
A. backstage: it is the area behind the stage and scenery, hidden from the audience.
B. balcony: it is a raised seating area for the audience, not part of the stage.
C. centre stage: it is the middle of the acting area, behind the curtain line.

Exam tip: learn the stage as a map, from back to front: backstage, upstage, centre stage, downstage, then the proscenium and apron, then the audience. Most questions on parts of the theatre are answered by placing the term on this map.

items.hint1: Look at what nature is doing in the sentence, and when it does it. Is the natural world reacting to a human event?
items.hint2: Hyperbole needs obvious exaggeration, and synecdoche uses a part to stand for the whole, as in 'hands' for workers. Neither describes nature reacting to a human event.
items.hint3: Choose between the device that shows nature sharing the feelings of a human event and the device that moves a describing word from a person to a thing, as in 'a sleepless night'. Which fits a violent wind at a murder?
items.solution:
Answer: B. pathetic fallacy

Pathetic fallacy is when nature, such as the weather, the sky or the sea, is shown as sharing or reacting to human feelings and events. Writers use it to make the natural world echo the mood of the story. (The stem prints 'kind', a misprint for 'king'.)

How to tell: the king is murdered, and at that moment 'the wind rose with a great violence'. The wind acts as if it is shocked and angry at the crime, so nature mirrors the human horror of the murder.

Why not the others:
A. hyperbole: it is deliberate exaggeration; a strong wind is possible, and the sentence does not overstate it for effect.
C. synecdoche: it uses a part for the whole, as in 'all hands on deck'; nothing here stands for something larger.
D. transferred epithet: it moves a describing word from a person to an object, as in 'a sleepless night'; here no describing word has been shifted.

Exam tip: if weather or nature seems to feel or react to what people are doing, especially at a death or a crime, think pathetic fallacy. Shakespeare's Macbeth does this: a wild storm rages on the night King Duncan is killed.

items.hint1: Look at the very first words of the extract, printed before anyone speaks. What kind of information do they give?
items.hint2: A curtain raiser is a short play performed before the main one, and an interlude is a short piece performed between parts of a play. Neither of these is a place.
items.hint3: Of the two options left, one is a kind of speech by a single speaker, and one is an element found in every story or play. Which one does 'Amponsah's residence' give you?
items.solution:
Answer: D. setting

Setting is the time and place in which the action of a story or play happens. In a play script, the setting is often printed at the head of a scene so that the reader and the director know where the action takes place.

How to tell: 'Amponsah's residence' is printed at the top, before anyone speaks. It names a place, Amponsah's house, and that is where Kwaku and Adwoa's exchange happens.

Why not the others:
A. curtain raiser: it is a short play performed before the main play, not a place.
B. dramatic monologue: it is a poem or long speech by one speaker to a silent listener; this is just a place name.
C. interlude: it is a short piece of entertainment between the parts of a play.

Exam tip: when a question points to words naming a house, a village, a time of day or a year, think setting. Setting answers two questions: where and when.

items.hint1: Think about the difference between the people written into a play and the real people who put it on stage.
items.hint2: Props are objects used on stage, such as a cup or a chair, and directors guide a performance without appearing in the script. Kwaku and Adwoa speak lines, so neither fits.
items.hint3: Now decide: are Kwaku and Adwoa people inside the story, or the real men and women who would play them in a performance? The question says 'in the extract'.
items.solution:
Answer: B. characters

Characters are the people, and sometimes animals or spirits, who take part in the action of a story or play. They exist in the script. Actors are the real people who take on those roles when the play is performed.

How to tell: the question says 'in the extract'. In the written extract, Kwaku and Adwoa are names in the script with lines to speak, so they are characters. The actors would be whoever plays them on a real stage.

Why not the others:
A. actors: they are the real performers on stage, not the named people inside the written text.
C. directors: they guide how a play is staged and do not appear as speakers in the script.
D. props: they are objects used on stage, such as a chair or a pot, not people.

Exam tip: in the text, it is a character; on the stage, playing the part, it is an actor. Watch for words like 'in the extract' or 'in the play' in the stem.

items.hint1: Think about who is meant to hear this line. Is Adwoa saying it to Kwaku, or saying it so that he does not hear?
items.hint2: A dialogue is a conversation between characters, and an ode is a kind of poem. This line is not a reply to Kwaku, and it is not a poem.
items.hint3: Two options let a character speak private thoughts. One is a long speech made when the character is alone; the other is a short remark slipped into a conversation that the other character does not hear. Which describes this line?
items.solution:
Answer: A. aside

An aside is a short remark a character makes to themselves or to the audience, which the other characters are taken not to hear. It lets the audience know what the character really thinks.

How to tell: Adwoa has just answered Kwaku politely, 'Right here, just a minute and I'll be with you'. Then she mutters a rude private thought that Kwaku is not meant to hear. It is short, and it comes in the middle of her exchange with him, so it is an aside.

Why not the others:
B. dialogue: it is conversation between characters; this line is not spoken to Kwaku.
C. ode: it is a formal poem of praise, not a line in a play.
D. soliloquy: it is a long speech a character makes when alone on stage, thinking aloud; this is a short remark made in the middle of a conversation.

Exam tip: short, private and in company points to an aside. Long, private and alone points to a soliloquy. Check the length of the speech and whether the character is in the middle of a conversation.

items.hint1: Look at how these words are printed in the extract, and ask whether any character actually says them aloud.
items.hint2: A curtain call happens at the end of a performance, when the actors come out to bow. A dress rehearsal is the last full practice before the first show. Neither is written inside a play script.
items.hint3: That leaves a piece of music played between scenes and a written instruction in the script. Is 'Muttering to herself' something the audience hears as music, or something that tells the actor how to act?
items.solution:
Answer: D. stage direction

A stage direction is an instruction written into a play script, usually in brackets or italics, telling the actors how to move or speak, or describing the scene. It is not spoken aloud.

How to tell: [Muttering to herself] is in brackets, no character speaks it, and it tells the actress playing Adwoa how to deliver the next line: quietly, to herself. The same extract has another one for Kwaku, [Pants for breath].

Why not the others:
A. curtain call: it is when the cast come on stage to bow at the end of a performance.
B. dress rehearsal: it is the final practice in full costume before the first show.
C. musical interlude: it is a short piece of music played between scenes or acts.

Exam tip: words in a play script that no character speaks, usually in brackets or italics, telling how to move, speak or feel, are stage directions.

items.hint1: The key word in the question is 'contrast'. Think of the character type whose main job is to make another character's qualities stand out.
items.hint2: The protagonist is the main character, and a clown is a comic character who makes the audience laugh. Neither is defined by contrast with someone else.
items.hint3: Choose between the character who fights against the main character and the character who is set beside another to show up their differences. The question asks about contrast, not conflict.
items.solution:
Answer: C. foil

A foil is a character whose qualities are very different from another character's, so that placing the two side by side makes the other character's traits clearer. A cowardly friend, for example, makes a brave hero look braver.

How to tell: the stem says the character 'serves as a contrast to another character'. Showing up another character through difference is the job of a foil.

Why not the others:
A. antagonist: this character opposes or struggles against the protagonist; the stress is on conflict, not on contrast.
B. clown: this is a comic character who amuses the audience.
D. protagonist: this is the main character of the work.

Exam tip: in conflict with the hero means antagonist; in contrast with another character means foil. A foil need not be an enemy; often it is a friend or a relative.

items.hint1: Read the sentence and ask whether the speaker says exactly what they mean, or says it in a softer way.
items.hint2: A limerick is a short, funny five-line poem, and a parody is a work that copies another in a mocking way. Neither is a device inside a single sentence.
items.hint3: Choose between a statement that seems to contradict itself but holds a truth, and a statement that makes its point by denying the opposite. Does 'not pleasant' contradict itself?
items.solution:
Answer: B. litotes

Litotes is understatement made by denying the opposite of what you mean. Instead of saying something is bad, you say it is 'not good'. It sounds calm or polite, while the listener still understands the stronger meaning.

How to tell: the speaker means the weather is bad. Instead of saying so directly, they say it is 'not pleasant', denying the opposite. That is litotes.

Why not the others:
A. limerick: it is a short, humorous poem of five lines, not a figure in a sentence.
C. paradox: it is a statement that seems to contradict itself but contains a truth, as in 'The child is father of the man'; 'not pleasant' contains no contradiction.
D. parody: it is a work that imitates another in a mocking or comic way.

Exam tip: look for 'not' or 'no' placed before a word of the opposite meaning: 'not bad', 'not unkind', 'no small matter'. That pattern signals litotes.

items.hint1: The key words are 'widely accepted'. Think of the term for the body of works that critics and teachers agree are the most important.
items.hint2: A database is a store of information, usually on a computer, and a period is a span of time in literary history. Neither names a group of accepted works.
items.hint3: Both remaining words can describe a group of works. Which one carries the idea of being widely accepted as important, and which one just means works gathered together?
items.solution:
Answer: A. canon

A canon is the body of literary works that critics, teachers and readers widely accept as important and of lasting value. Works in the canon are the ones most often studied and taught, such as Shakespeare's plays or Chinua Achebe's 'Things Fall Apart'.

How to tell: the stem stresses works that are 'widely accepted'. That wide acceptance is what makes a work part of the canon. A plain collection does not need it.

Why not the others:
B. compilation: it is any collection of works put together, whether or not they are highly regarded.
C. database: it is a store of information, often on a computer, not a literary term.
D. period: it is a span of time in literary history, such as the Romantic period.

Exam tip: widely accepted, classic or standard works make up the canon; a book of poems by several writers is an anthology. Learn these collection words together.

items.hint1: Picture the speaker walking into the room. How does she carry herself, and how do the men around her react?
items.hint2: 'Just as cool as you please' shows calm and ease. The men's reaction shows they are impressed by her, and she says nothing to insult them.
items.hint3: Impunity means acting as if you will never be punished, and nothing in the lines suggests wrongdoing. Of the two options left, do the lines show her love for the men, or a strong belief in herself?
items.solution:
Answer: D. exudes self confidence

To exude a quality is to show it plainly, as if it flows out of you. Self confidence is a firm belief in your own worth. A speaker who describes herself as calm and describes others reacting strongly to her is showing that belief.

How to tell: she walks in 'Just as cool as you please', calm and at ease, and the men 'stand or / Fall down on their knees' at the sight of her. She is sure of the effect she has. These lines come from Maya Angelou's poem 'Phenomenal Woman', which celebrates a woman's pride in herself.

Why not the others:
A. adores men: she describes the men's reaction to her, not her love for them.
B. disrespects men: she does not insult or look down on them; she simply reports how they respond.
C. exhibits impunity: impunity means freedom from punishment, and she has done nothing wrong that could be punished.

Exam tip: to judge what a speaker is like, look first at how they describe their own actions and manner, then at how others react to them.

items.hint1: Look at the two reactions of the men in this line. Are they alike or different?
items.hint2: Apostrophe is speaking directly to someone absent or to a thing, and metonymy uses something closely linked to a thing to stand for it, as in 'the crown' for the king. The line does neither.
items.hint3: Choose between setting two opposite things side by side and repeating the same grammatical pattern. Is 'stand' against 'fall down on their knees' a repeated pattern, or two opposite positions?
items.solution:
Answer: B. contrast

Contrast is placing two opposite or very different things side by side so that the difference stands out. Here the opposite reactions show how strongly the men are affected by the speaker.

How to tell: 'stand' means rising upright, and 'fall down on their knees' means sinking low. The two reactions are opposites, joined by 'or'. Either way the men are struck by her, and the opposite positions make that clear.

Why not the others:
A. apostrophe: it is speaking directly to someone absent or to a thing, as in 'O Death'; the speaker addresses no one here.
C. metonymy: it names something by a thing closely linked to it, as in 'the crown' for the king; no such swap happens.
D. parallelism: it repeats the same grammatical structure in matching phrases, as in 'I came, I saw, I conquered'; the single verb 'stand' and the longer phrase 'fall down on their knees' do not form a matching pattern.

Exam tip: if a line puts two opposite things side by side (up and down, rich and poor, laugh and cry), think contrast. Choose parallelism when the same sentence pattern is clearly repeated.

items.hint1: This is an analogy. First work out the link in the first pair: what is a chapter to a novel or other prose work?
items.hint2: A chapter is one main section of a prose work. You need the matching main section of a poem. Act and scene belong to a different genre altogether.
items.hint3: Is a line the size of a chapter, or closer to the size of a sentence? Which remaining option names the larger section that matches a chapter?
items.solution:
Answer: D. stanza

Each genre is divided into units. Prose is divided into chapters, drama into acts and scenes, and poetry into stanzas, which are groups of lines set apart by a space. A stanza does in a poem what a chapter does in a novel: it marks off one main section.

How to tell: a chapter is a main division of prose. The matching main division of a poem is the stanza.

Why not the others:
A. act: it is a main division of a play, so it belongs to drama.
B. line: it is a single row of words in a poem, closer to a sentence than a chapter.
C. scene: it is a smaller division within an act of a play, so it also belongs to drama.

Exam tip: in 'A is to B as C is to D' questions, state the link in the first pair as a short sentence ('a chapter is a main section of prose'), then test each option with the same sentence.

items.hint1: Look at the verb in the title. What does the sea do to the land, and is that something a sea can really do?
items.hint2: Chiasmus reverses word order in two balanced halves, and an epithet is a describing word or phrase attached to a name, such as 'swift-footed Achilles'. The title has neither.
items.hint3: Two options give nature a living quality. One shows nature sharing human feelings to match a human event; the other gives a thing the actions of a living being. Is 'eats' a feeling or an action?
items.solution:
Answer: D. personification

Personification gives a non-living thing, such as the sea, human qualities or the actions of a living being. It makes the thing seem alive and able to act on purpose.

How to tell: eating is something living creatures do. By saying the sea 'Eats' the land, the title makes the sea act like a hungry creature. In plain terms it describes the waves wearing away the coast. This is the title of Kofi Awoonor's poem about the sea destroying a coastal home.

Why not the others:
A. chiasmus: it reverses the order of words in two balanced parts; nothing is reversed in the title.
B. epithet: it is a describing word or phrase attached to a name, such as 'swift-footed Achilles'; the title contains no such label.
C. fallacy: read as pathetic fallacy, it shows nature sharing human feelings at a human event; here the sea is given an action, not an emotion that echoes a human mood.

Exam tip: if a thing does something a living being does (eats, weeps, whispers, sleeps), think personification first. Choose pathetic fallacy when nature's mood matches the human mood of the scene.

items.hint1: Pick out the strongest words the speaker uses about how the animals are treated and who is to blame. They tell you the feeling behind the speech.
items.hint2: The speaker blames man for the animals' misery, so he does not feel guilty himself. He talks about man to the other animals, and he does not hurl insults at his listeners.
items.hint3: Choose between a speaker who preaches about good conduct in general and a speaker burning with indignation at cruelty and theft. Which feeling do 'hideous cruelty' and 'stolen from us' carry?
items.solution:
Answer: B. angry

Tone is the speaker's attitude, and we find it in the words he chooses. Strong, charged words about cruelty and injustice, aimed at a clearly named enemy, show anger.

How to tell: the speaker says the animals are 'slaughtered with hideous cruelty', that their produce is 'stolen from us', and that 'Man is the only real enemy that we have'. These are the words of someone furious at how they are treated. The passage is Old Major's speech in George Orwell's 'Animal Farm'.

Why not the others:
A. abusive: an abusive speaker hurls insults; he condemns what man does but does not call anyone names.
C. moralistic: a moralistic speaker preaches about good manners and right conduct in general; this speech is a furious charge against a named oppressor.
D. guilty: he blames man for the animals' misery and takes no blame on himself.

Exam tip: to name a tone, underline the three or four most emotional words in the passage and ask what feeling they share. Words like 'cruelty', 'stolen' and 'enemy' point to anger.

items.hint1: Ask whether the phrase is meant literally. Can strength really be measured in atoms?
items.hint2: Metonymy uses a linked thing to stand for something, and antithesis balances two opposite ideas in matching phrases. The phrase has no swap and no pair of opposites.
items.hint3: Choose between saying the opposite of what you mean and stretching the truth to stress a point. Does 'the last atom' say the opposite of hard work, or push the idea of hard work to its extreme?
items.solution:
Answer: B. hyperbole

Hyperbole is deliberate exaggeration used for emphasis. The speaker does not expect to be taken literally; the overstatement makes the point hit harder.

How to tell: an atom is far too tiny to see. Saying the animals work 'to the last atom of our strength' means they are worked until nothing at all is left. It is an overstatement to stress how cruelly they are overworked.

Why not the others:
A. antithesis: it sets opposite ideas in balanced phrases, as in 'Speech is silver, silence is golden'; the phrase has no pair of opposites.
C. irony: it says one thing while meaning the opposite; the speaker means exactly that they are overworked.
D. metonymy: it replaces a thing with something closely linked to it, as in 'the pen' for writing; nothing is replaced here.

Exam tip: if a phrase would be impossible or absurd taken literally, and it makes a fact or feeling sound bigger, think hyperbole. Look for phrases like 'the last atom', 'a million times' or 'tons of'.

items.hint1: Read the sentence that comes straight after the question. Who answers it?
items.hint2: An adage is an old, well-known saying, such as a proverb, and sarcasm is mocking language that means the opposite of what it says. The question is neither a proverb nor mockery.
items.hint3: Choose between a question that asks the reader to work something out from clues and a question asked for effect that the speaker answers himself. Look again at the word 'Because' that follows.
items.solution:
Answer: C. a rhetorical question

A rhetorical question is asked for effect, not to get an answer from the listener. Speakers use it to draw attention to a point, and they often answer it themselves straight away.

How to tell: the speaker asks 'Why then do we continue in these miserable conditions?' and at once answers it himself: 'Because nearly the whole of the produce of our labour is stolen from us by human beings.' He does not wait for the animals to reply. He uses the question to lead them to his point.

Why not the others:
A. an adage: it is an old, widely known saying, such as 'Make hay while the sun shines'.
B. an inference question: it asks the reader to work out an answer from clues; here the speaker supplies the answer himself.
D. a sarcasm: it is mocking language that says one thing and means the opposite; the question is serious.

Exam tip: in a speech, if a question is followed at once by the speaker's own answer, or needs no answer at all, it is a rhetorical question.

items.hint1: Ask what the speaker wants his listeners to understand by the end of the speech, and how he goes about it.
items.hint2: The language is formal, like a speech at a meeting, so it is not casual everyday talk. Nothing in it is meant to make anyone laugh.
items.hint3: Choose between a voice built on figures of speech and a voice that explains a problem and its cause to the listeners. Look at 'This, comrades is the answer to all our problems'. Which describes the speaker's voice?
items.solution:
Answer: C. didactic

A didactic voice teaches or instructs. The speaker sets out to explain something to the listeners and lead them to a lesson or a course of action.

How to tell: the speaker describes the animals' misery, asks why it happens, explains the cause (man steals the produce of their labour), and tells them what follows: 'This, comrades is the answer to all our problems.' He is teaching his comrades why they suffer and what must be done about it.

Why not the others:
A. colloquial: a colloquial voice uses casual, everyday talk; this is formal speech-making.
B. comical: nothing in the passage is meant to amuse; the subject is suffering and death.
D. metaphoric: there are a few figurative touches, such as 'root cause', but they do not define the voice; the speech is mainly plain explanation.

Exam tip: if a speaker explains a problem, gives its cause and tells the listeners what to do or believe, the voice is didactic. Didactic means 'meant to teach'.

items.hint1: Read the line as a promise. Is the speaker looking back at the past, or forward to the future?
items.hint2: The line says hunger and overwork will end, which is good news for the animals. So despair does not fit, and nothing in the line threatens the listeners.
items.hint3: Choose between a feeling of malice towards man and a feeling of eager hope for what is coming. Where does the line put its weight: on man, or on the better life after him?
items.solution:
Answer: A. expectancy

Expectancy is the eager feeling of waiting for something good that you believe will come. A promise of a better future raises that feeling in listeners.

How to tell: the speaker says that if man is removed, 'the root cause of hunger and overwork is abolished forever'. For animals who have just heard how miserable their lives are, this is a promise of a future without hunger and overwork. It makes them look forward with hope.

Why not the others:
B. fear: nothing in the line threatens the animals; it promises relief.
C. hopelessness: the line does the opposite, offering a way out of their misery.
D. spite: the line does call for removing man, but its focus is the good life that follows, not a wish to hurt man.

Exam tip: for 'what feeling does this line evoke' questions, check whether the line looks forward or back, and whether what it describes is good or bad for the listeners. A good future points to hope or expectancy.

items.hint1: Think about the length of the poem, who is speaking, and whether it tells a long story or expresses a personal feeling.
items.hint2: An epic is a very long poem about a hero's great deeds, and a dirge is a sad song for the dead. This short poem addressed to 'my Alberta' is neither.
items.hint3: Choose between a formal, elevated poem of praise and a short poem in which the speaker shares his own private feelings. Which fits a speaker thinking about someone dear to him?
items.solution:
Answer: C. a lyrics

A lyric is a short poem in which a single speaker expresses personal thoughts and feelings, often about love, loss or nature. It focuses on emotion rather than on telling a long story. (The option prints 'a lyrics', a misprint for 'a lyric'.)

How to tell: the poem is short, spoken by one 'I', and addressed to 'my Alberta'. The speaker does not tell a story of great deeds or mourn a death; he shares his own private feelings about when he will see her again.

Why not the others:
A. adirge: a dirge (the option runs 'a' and 'dirge' together) is a sad song of mourning for the dead; Alberta is alive, and the speaker hopes to see her again.
B. an epic: it is a very long narrative poem about a hero's deeds.
D. an ode: it is a formal, elevated poem of praise, often to a person or object; this poem is private and personal rather than grand and ceremonial.

Exam tip: short, one speaker and personal feelings point to a lyric. Long, with a hero's deeds, points to an epic. Mourning the dead points to a dirge or elegy. Formal praise points to an ode.

items.hint1: Focus on what the speaker wants. Read the last three lines, where he imagines what he will do while awake in bed.
items.hint2: Nothing in the poem shows the speaker is cross with Alberta or thanking her for something. The feeling is about wanting her near.
items.hint3: Choose between a steady, loyal, almost worshipful attachment and a strong longing to see and touch someone. Which fits a speaker who imagines he will 'hold and fondle' her?
items.solution:
Answer: B. desire

Desire is a strong wish or longing for someone or something, often including a longing to be physically close. In love poems it shows in words about wanting to see, hear and touch the loved one.

How to tell: the speaker longs for the day his eyes 'will rest a while' on Alberta's smile again, and at night he imagines he will 'hold and fondle' her 'velvety texture'. These are words of wanting to be near her and to touch her, which is desire.

Why not the others:
A. anger: nothing in the poem shows resentment towards Alberta.
C. devotion: it suggests steady, loyal, almost worshipful attachment; the poem stresses physical longing rather than loyalty.
D. gratitude: the speaker is not thanking Alberta for anything.

Exam tip: when two feelings seem close, pick the one the strongest verbs support. Touch words like 'hold' and 'fondle' point to desire; words of service, faith or loyalty point to devotion.

items.hint1: Look at how the two quoted parts are built. Compare the words in the same positions in each part.
items.hint2: Each part may carry its own image, but the question quotes the two parts together. Look for what they share rather than what either one means alone.
items.hint3: Choose between repeating the same first consonant sound and repeating the same sentence pattern. Line up 'My eyes will rest' and 'My ears will drink' word by word: what repeats?
items.solution:
Answer: C. parallelism

Parallelism is the use of the same grammatical pattern in two or more phrases or lines, so that they match in shape. It creates balance and rhythm and links the ideas together.

How to tell: set the two parts one above the other.
My eyes will rest
My ears will drink
Each follows the same pattern: 'My' + a sense organ + 'will' + a verb. The repeated shape is parallelism.

Why not the others:
A. alliteration: it repeats consonant sounds at the start of nearby words; the question is about the matching pattern of two whole phrases, not a run of sounds.
B. metaphor: 'ears will drink' on its own is figurative, but the question sets the two parts together, and what they share is their pattern, not a comparison.
D. simile: it compares using 'like' or 'as', and neither part uses them.

Exam tip: when a question quotes two or more phrases together, line them up word by word. If the same grammatical pattern repeats, think parallelism.

items.hint1: Go through the poem and note every word linked to one of the five senses: seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching.
items.hint2: No word in the poem is about a smell or a taste, so two options fall away.
items.hint3: The contest is between hearing and one other sense. Count the phrases for each, including lines that are repeated, and see which sense keeps coming back.
items.solution:
Answer: B. sight

Imagery is language that appeals to the senses. When a poem keeps returning to one sense, that sense dominates its imagery. Images of sight are called visual images.

How to tell: sort the images by sense.
Sight: 'brightness of smile', 'softness of smile', 'My eyes will rest a while' (twice), 'silver moonshine', 'mirage'.
Hearing: 'softness of voice' (printed as 'voce').
Touch: 'hold and fondle', 'velvety texture'.
Smell and taste: none.
Sight has by far the most.

Why not the others:
A. hearing: there is one image of sound, 'softness of voice', against many images of seeing.
C. smell: no word in the poem appeals to smell.
D. taste: no word in the poem appeals to taste.

Exam tip: for dominant imagery questions, jot the sense words under five headings in the margin and count. Count a repeated line each time it appears.

items.hint1: Read the quoted lines word by word and ask whether the speaker believes the holding and fondling will be real.
items.hint2: Didactic means teaching a lesson, and pedantic means showing off learning or being fussy about small details. The lines do neither.
items.hint3: Choose between vivid, stage-like action and a gloomy sense that things will not turn out well. What do the words 'dreaming', 'delusions' and 'mirage' say about his hopes?
items.solution:
Answer: D. pessimistic

A pessimistic tone expects the worst or doubts that things will turn out well. In a love poem it shows when the speaker admits that what he longs for may not happen.

How to tell: the speaker will hold Alberta only while 'dreaming', and what he holds are 'delusions' and a 'mirage', things that are not real. The poem also opens 'I know not' when he will see her again. He knows his longing will not be met in reality, which gives the lines a gloomy, doubtful note.

Why not the others:
A. didactic: a didactic tone teaches a lesson; the speaker shares private feelings and instructs no one.
B. dramatic: the image is vivid, but 'dramatic' does not name the speaker's attitude, and the key words cut the fantasy down rather than build it up.
C. pedantic: a pedantic tone is fussy about small details or shows off learning; nothing here does.

Exam tip: in tone questions, words about illusion or unreality (dream, delusion, mirage, shadow) often signal doubt or disappointment. Check whether the speaker believes his hope will come true.

items.hint1: Ask two things: who would need to argue that he is as good a match as another man, and who is being called 'my lord'. In this play, 'my lord' is how people speak to someone of high rank.
items.hint2: The speaker talks about his own love and his own right, so he must be a young man who wants to marry. That rules out Egeus, the old father, as the speaker, and Theseus, who is hearing the case and has no rival in love here.
items.hint3: Two options are left. Look at each pair and ask whether the listener could be called 'my lord'. Then check that the speaker is a young man pleading his own case.
items.solution:
Answer: C. Lysander and Theseus

To find the speaker and the person addressed, use the clues inside the lines: how the speaker names the listener, and what the speaker wants. Here the speaker calls the listener 'my lord' and argues that his own birth, wealth and love are as good as another man's.

How to tell: this is Act 1 Scene 1. Egeus has asked Duke Theseus to force his daughter Hermia to marry Demetrius. Lysander, who loves Hermia, answers by telling the Duke that he is 'as well derived' (as well born) as his rival, and that Hermia loves him. 'My lord' is the Duke.

Why not the others:
A. Demetrius and Hermia: Demetrius is the rival being compared, not the speaker, and nobody would call Hermia 'my lord'.
B. Egeus and Helena: Egeus is Hermia's father and is not claiming to be loved, and Helena is not the one being spoken to.
D. Theseus and Egeus: Theseus is the judge hearing the case, so he is the one addressed, not the speaker.

Exam tip: in a 'speaker and addressee' question, look first at how the listener is named ('my lord', 'father', 'sweet') and then at what the speaker wants. Together they usually point to one pair.

items.hint1: 'He' points back to a man the speaker is comparing himself with. Read on to 'my love is more than his' and ask who the speaker is competing against.
items.hint2: 'He' is one man, so an option naming two people cannot fit. The speaker also cannot be comparing himself with himself.
items.hint3: Two single men are left: an old father who brought the complaint, and a young man who also wants to marry Hermia. Whose birth, wealth and love would a suitor measure himself against?
items.solution:
Answer: A. Demetrius

A pronoun such as 'he' in an extract points back to someone already being discussed in the scene. Here the speaker, Lysander, is weighing himself against his rival for Hermia, man against man.

How to tell: the lines compare birth ('as well derived'), wealth ('as well possessed') and love ('my love is more than his'). Those are the grounds on which two suitors compete. Egeus wants Hermia to marry Demetrius, so Demetrius is the man Lysander must prove himself equal to. In the full text the blank in the fourth line is his name: 'If not with vantage, as Demetrius''.

Why not the others:
B. Eqeus: Egeus is Hermia's father, not a suitor, so he has no love for Hermia to compare.
C. Lysander: Lysander is the speaker, the 'I' of the line, so he cannot also be 'he'.
D. Theseus and Egeus: 'he' is one person, and neither of these men is competing for Hermia.

Exam tip: when asked what a pronoun refers to, check number first (one person or more), then rule out the speaker ('I'), then ask who fits the comparison being made.

items.hint1: The play moves between two places: the city, with its court and its laws, and the wood outside it, where the fairies rule. Decide which world this speech belongs to.
items.hint2: This speech is part of a formal hearing: a claim is argued before a ruler, with a father's complaint in the background. Think about where such a hearing would be held.
items.hint3: Three of the options are ways of naming the wood. Decide whether this scene comes before or after the lovers run away, and choose from there.
items.solution:
Answer: B. Athens

A Midsummer Night's Dream opens in Athens, at the palace of Duke Theseus, and only later moves into the wood near the city. The scenes about law, marriage choices and the Duke's judgement belong to Athens. The scenes of fairy magic belong to the wood.

How to tell: this speech comes from Act 1 Scene 1. Egeus has brought his complaint to Theseus, and Lysander argues his claim to Hermia in front of the Duke. Only after Theseus rules against them do Lysander and Hermia plan to escape to the wood.

Why not the others:
A. another part of the wood: this names the setting of later scenes, after the lovers have fled.
C. a wood near Athens: this is the setting of the fairy scenes from Act 2 onward, not of the opening hearing.
D. the wood: the lovers are not yet in the wood when this speech is made.

Exam tip: for a setting question on a Shakespeare extract, first place the extract in the story, then ask which location that part of the play uses. When several options are versions of one place, check whether the scene is in that place at all.

items.hint1: Look for the question the speaker asks himself in the middle of the speech. It tells you what he is trying to do.
items.hint2: He praises his birth, his wealth and his love. Someone accepting blame or trying to make peace would not boast like this.
items.hint3: Narrow to resisting arrest and defending his right. Is anyone trying to arrest him in these lines, or is he arguing a claim?
items.solution:
Answer: B. defending his right

To say what a speaker is doing in an extract, look at the purpose of his words: is he attacking, pleading, apologising or claiming something? Lysander is making a case for himself before the Duke.

How to tell: he lists his good birth, his wealth and Hermia's love for him, then asks, 'Why should not I then prosecute my right?' To 'prosecute my right' means to press his claim. His right is his claim to marry Hermia, which Egeus is trying to block.

Why not the others:
A. accepting blame: he admits no fault and instead attacks his rival as 'spotted and inconstant'.
C. resisting arrest: nobody is trying to arrest him, he is arguing before a judge.
D. seeking reconciliation: he is not trying to make peace with Egeus or his rival, he is arguing against them.

Exam tip: when a question asks what a speaker is doing, find the one line that states the speaker's aim, often a question or a demand, and match the option to it.

items.hint1: 'Nedar's daughter' names a young woman by her father. Think about which women in the play are ordinary Athenians and which are queens.
items.hint2: Hippolyta is Queen of the Amazons and Titania is Queen of the Fairies. Neither is the young woman the extract describes.
items.hint3: Narrow to the two young Athenian women. The extract says Nedar's daughter still dotes on a man who deserted her. Which of the two is in that position when the play opens?
items.solution:
Answer: A. Helena

Shakespeare often names a character through a family tie, such as 'Nedar's daughter'. Knowing each young woman's father helps you tell Hermia and Helena apart, which many students confuse.

How to tell: Lysander says that Demetrius courted Nedar's daughter, won her heart, and then turned away from her, and that she still 'dotes' on him. That is Helena, who goes on loving Demetrius although he now wants Hermia.

Why not the others:
B. Hermia: she is the daughter of Egeus, and she is the woman Lysander and Demetrius are competing for.
C. Hippolyta: she is Queen of the Amazons, soon to marry Theseus.
D. Titania: she is Queen of the Fairies, the wife of Oberon.

Exam tip: learn the family ties of the main characters as pairs, such as Hermia and Egeus, Helena and Nedar. Questions that name a character by a father or husband test exactly these links.

items.hint1: This is a spell, spoken in short rhyming lines. Think about which characters in the play hold magic power and use it on others.
items.hint2: The first and second fairy are servants who sing a lullaby to keep harmful creatures away from a sleeper. This speech does the opposite: it welcomes whatever creature appears.
items.hint3: Narrow to the fairy king and Puck, his servant. Recall which of the two gives the orders about the magic flower in Act 2, and whose plan this charm carries out.
items.solution:
Answer: B. oberon

In A Midsummer Night's Dream the love-juice is the juice of a magic flower that makes a sleeper fall in love with the first creature they see on waking. Two characters use it with a spoken charm: Oberon, the fairy king, and Puck, his servant. Each charm has its own words, so the words tell you the speaker.

How to tell: this is the charm Oberon speaks in Act 2 Scene 2 as he squeezes the juice onto Titania's eyelids. It names wild beasts, the ounce (a lynx), cat, bear, pard (leopard) and boar, and ends 'Wake when some vile thing is near'. Puck's charm later in the same scene is different: it begins 'Churl, upon thy eyes I throw' and is spoken over Lysander.

Why not the others:
A. first fairy: the fairies sing a lullaby to keep harmful creatures away, the opposite of this charm.
C. puck: his charm in this scene has different words and is spoken over an Athenian man.
D. second fairy: the second fairy also only sings in the lullaby and has no love-juice.

Exam tip: learn the special words of the play's charms and songs and who speaks each. A list of wild beasts points to one charm, a 'churl' to another.

items.hint1: The first line speaks to someone who will 'wake' later. Ask what the speaker could be doing to a sleeping person while saying these words.
items.hint2: Nobody proposes to someone who is asleep, and the magic flower has already been fetched before this moment.
items.hint3: Narrow to pouring the potion and reversing his mistake. Has any mistake with the love-juice been made yet at this point in the play?
items.solution:
Answer: B. pouring the potion

A charm in a play is usually spoken while the magic is being done, so its words describe what the magic will cause. This charm tells the sleeper what they will love on waking, which means the love-juice is being put on their eyes as it is spoken.

How to tell: in Act 2 Scene 2 Oberon finds Titania asleep and squeezes the juice of the flower onto her eyelids, saying 'What thou seest when thou dost wake, Do it for thy true-love take'. The examiner calls this 'pouring the potion'.

Why not the others:
A. picking herbs: Puck fetched the flower earlier, in Act 2 Scene 1, so it is already in Oberon's hand.
C. proposing to Helena: nobody proposes in this charm, and Oberon does not court Helena in the play.
D. reversing his mistake: the mistakes with the love-juice come later, and they are put right in Acts 3 and 4, not here.

Exam tip: when asked what a speaker is doing, look for words that only make sense alongside an action, such as talking to a sleeper about waking. Then check the order of events so you do not pick something that happens earlier or later.

items.hint1: A motive is the reason behind an action. Read the last line of the charm and ask what the speaker hopes will happen to the sleeper.
items.hint2: Look at the creatures listed: a lynx, a bear, a leopard, a boar with bristled hair, and 'some vile thing'. Nobody who wants to forgive someone, or who needs their love, wishes this on them.
items.hint3: Narrow to the desire to please and the desire to punish. Ask whose wishes the charm serves, the sleeper's or the speaker's, and what it will cost the sleeper.
items.solution:
Answer: B. the desire to punish

A character's motive is the reason for what they do. Oberon charms Titania because she has refused to give him the changeling, the little Indian boy he wants as his page. He means to pay her back by making her love something ugly and foolish.

How to tell: the charm hopes she will wake to love a wild beast, and ends 'Wake when some vile thing is near'. Earlier, in Act 2 Scene 1, Oberon says she shall not leave the grove till he torments her 'for this injury'. The aim is to shame her until she gives way.

Why not the others:
A. the desire to please: a charm that wishes a 'vile thing' on her is not meant to please her.
C. the need to forgive: he is angry with her, and the charm is revenge, not forgiveness.
D. the need to love: the charm is not an act of love, it is meant to humiliate her.

Exam tip: to find a motive, set the speaker's words against what has just happened between the characters. A wish for something 'vile' after a quarrel points to revenge.

items.hint1: The speaker's action is the charm itself. Think about the order in which the love-juice is used in the play and who receives it first.
items.hint2: Helena is not given the love-juice at any point in the play. Demetrius gets it only in Act 3, with a charm that begins 'Flower of this purple dye'.
items.hint3: Narrow to Lysander and Titania, both asleep in the wood in the same scene. Recall which of them is charmed by the speaker himself, and which by his servant.
items.solution:
Answer: D. Titania

Oberon uses the love-juice first on his own queen, Titania, as revenge in their quarrel. He then sends Puck to use it on an Athenian man, which leads to the mix-ups among the young lovers.

How to tell: in Act 2 Scene 2 Titania's fairies sing her to sleep in her bower. Oberon then squeezes the juice on her eyelids with this charm, hoping she will wake to love a beast. She wakes and falls for Bottom, who has been given an ass's head.

Why not the others:
A. Demetrius: he is charmed later, in Act 3, with a different charm that begins 'Flower of this purple dye'.
B. Helena: she is not given the love-juice at all; the charmed men fall in love with her.
C. Lysander: he is charmed by Puck, not Oberon, with a charm that begins 'Churl, upon thy eyes I throw'.

Exam tip: for 'at whom is the action directed' questions, list the uses of the magic in the play in order: who uses it, on whom, and with what words. Each charm in this play fits one victim.

items.hint1: Think about the bond between the speaker and the sleeper outside this one scene: what are they to each other in the fairy world?
items.hint2: Courtiers are people who attend a ruler at court, and these two are the rulers themselves. 'Friends' is too weak a word for the bond between them.
items.hint3: Narrow to enemies and lovers. They are quarrelling bitterly at this moment. Ask whether a quarrel cancels the bond between them, and how things stand between them by the end of the play.
items.solution:
Answer: D. lovers

Oberon and Titania are the King and Queen of the Fairies, and husband and wife. The examiner uses 'lovers' in the loose sense of a couple bound by love and marriage, even though at this point in the play they are quarrelling.

How to tell: their quarrel is over the changeling boy, and Oberon's charm is a way of getting back at his wife. But a quarrel between husband and wife does not make them enemies. In Act 4 Oberon frees Titania from the charm and they make peace and dance together, and at the end they bless the marriages together.

Why not the others:
A. courtiers: courtiers serve a king and queen, and these two are the king and queen.
B. enemies: they are at odds for a time, but they are a married couple who make peace, not true enemies.
C. friends: this word misses the fact that they are husband and wife.

Exam tip: when asked how two characters are related, choose the lasting relationship, such as husband and wife or father and daughter, not the mood of one scene. A quarrel is a stage in a relationship, not the relationship itself.

items.hint1: Look for a phrase in which the speaker describes their own patience. It tells you what kind of person is speaking.
items.hint2: 'Maiden's patience' means the speaker is a young unmarried woman. That rules out Oberon, and Titania is a married queen who plays no part in this quarrel among the young people.
items.hint3: Narrow to the two young Athenian women. Ask which of them, at this point in the wood, has lost track of the man she loves and fears the worst.
items.solution:
Answer: B. Hermia

In Act 3 Scene 2 Hermia has woken in the wood to find Lysander gone. When she meets Demetrius, she suspects he has killed Lysander in his sleep, and she turns on him in fury.

How to tell: 'maiden's patience' shows the speaker is a young unmarried woman. She asks 'Hast thou slain him, then?' and 'hast thou killed him sleeping?', so she believes someone she loves has been murdered. Of the options, only Hermia is in that position.

Why not the others:
A. Helena: she accuses no one of murder in the play, and the man she loves is not missing.
C. Oberon: he is a man and the fairy king, not a maiden, and he watches this scene unseen.
D. Titania: she is a married queen, and she is away in her bower with Bottom, not in this quarrel.

Exam tip: look for words in which a speaker describes themselves, such as 'maiden', 'father' or 'king'. They cut down the options before you need to remember the scene.

items.hint1: The addressee is the 'thou' of the speech, the person the speaker is facing and calling a dog, a cur and a serpent. Ask who is with her in the wood at this point.
items.hint2: Egeus is not in the wood during this scene, and Oberon is invisible to the humans, so she cannot be speaking to either of them.
items.hint3: Narrow to the two young Athenian men. Which of them is following the speaker through the wood, still asking for her love, when she turns on him?
items.solution:
Answer: A. Demetrius

The addressee is the person the speaker is talking to, here marked by 'thou' and 'thine'. In Act 3 Scene 2 Demetrius has followed Hermia into the wood, still hoping to win her, and she blames him for Lysander's disappearance.

How to tell: she asks 'thou' whether he has killed 'him' while he slept. The 'him' is Lysander, so the man in front of her must be someone else. The man with her at this moment is Demetrius, her unwanted suitor and Lysander's rival.

Why not the others:
B. Eqeus: Egeus, Hermia's father, is not in the wood in this scene.
C. Oberon: he watches unseen with Puck, so Hermia cannot see him to speak to him.
D. Lysander: he is the man she thinks has been killed, so he is the 'him', not the 'thou'.

Exam tip: in an angry speech, separate 'thou' (the person being blamed, who is present) from 'him' or 'her' (the person being talked about, who is absent). In an extract like this, the addressee is the 'thou'.

items.hint1: 'Him' in 'Hast thou slain him' is someone absent whom the speaker cares about. Think about who has gone missing in the wood at this point.
items.hint2: Thisby is only a part in the workmen's play, not a real person in the wood, and the man being spoken to cannot be the one who has been slain.
items.hint3: Narrow to Bottom and the speaker's own sweetheart. Whose absence would the speaker notice on waking, and whom would she fear her rival suitor had killed?
items.solution:
Answer: C. Lysander

In Act 3 Scene 2 Puck's charm has made Lysander fall in love with Helena, and he has left Hermia asleep in the wood to follow her. Hermia wakes, finds him gone, and fears he has been killed.

How to tell: she asks the man before her, 'Hast thou slain him, then? And hast thou killed him sleeping?' Lysander was sleeping near her when she last saw him, and Demetrius is his rival, so she assumes Demetrius has murdered him. In fact Lysander is alive, which is why the question says 'supposedly'.

Why not the others:
A. Bottom: he is with Titania, wearing an ass's head, and nobody thinks he is dead.
B. Demetrius: he is the man she is accusing, not the one she thinks was slain.
D. Thisby: she is a character in the workmen's play, acted by Flute, and has no part in this scene.

Exam tip: when a stem says 'supposedly', the event did not really happen. Ask who believes it and why, and look for the person that character is most afraid for.

items.hint1: Decide what the speaker is doing with the word 'serpent': comparing one thing to another, speaking to something absent, or letting a part stand for a whole.
items.hint2: Synecdoche uses a part to stand for the whole, as in 'hands' for workers, and no part stands for anything here. A conceit is a long, surprising comparison between very unlike things, worked out at length, not a single name.
items.hint3: Narrow to apostrophe and metaphor. Remember what apostrophe needs: an absent, dead or non-human listener spoken to as if present. Is that what happens when the speaker calls the man in front of her a serpent?
items.solution:
Answer: C. metaphor

A metaphor says one thing is another, without 'like' or 'as', to carry over its qualities. Calling a man a serpent gives him the snake's qualities: sly, two-faced and deadly.

How to tell: Hermia calls Demetrius 'thou serpent'. She does not say he is like a serpent, she names him one. The 'doubler tongue' plays on a snake's forked tongue to suggest that he is a liar.

Why not the others:
A. apostrophe: apostrophe addresses someone absent, dead or not human as if they could hear, but Demetrius is present and is the one she is speaking to.
B. conceit: in the syllabus a conceit is an extended, surprising comparison between very unlike things, and a liar as a snake is a common, direct image.
D. synecdoche: synecdoche uses a part for the whole, such as 'hands' for workers, and nothing here is a part standing for a whole.

Exam tip: when a line calls a person by the name of an animal or thing, test for metaphor first. Choose apostrophe only if the one being spoken to is absent, dead or not a person.

items.hint1: Read the two questions the speaker asks in the second and third lines. An accusation is often put as a question.
items.hint2: Bottom is alive and nobody in this scene mentions him, and nothing in the extract speaks of broken promises or unfaithfulness.
items.hint3: Narrow to being unfair and a killing. Do her questions complain about how she has been treated in general, or name one particular deed?
items.solution:
Answer: D. killing Lysander

An accusation names a wrong that the speaker says someone has done. Hermia blames Demetrius for one particular deed: the murder of Lysander.

How to tell: she asks 'Hast thou slain him, then? And hast thou killed him sleeping?', and says no adder ever stung with a more forked tongue than his. 'Him' is Lysander, whom she woke to find missing. She is wrong, since Lysander has only gone off after Helena, but that is her accusation.

Why not the others:
A. being unfair: this is too general, and she names a specific crime.
B. being unfaithful: Demetrius was unfaithful to Helena, but that is not what Hermia charges him with here.
C. killing Bottom: Bottom is not dead and has nothing to do with this quarrel.

Exam tip: for 'the speaker accuses the addressee of' questions, look for the verb in the speaker's questions or charges, such as 'slain' or 'killed', and pick the option that names that deed and its victim.

items.hint1: Quince stands before the audience and introduces the play and each of the actors in turn. Think about the name for the speech that opens a play and explains what is coming.
items.hint2: Quince points to the other players, 'This man' and 'This beauteous lady', and tells the audience which part each plays. He is not appearing as a character inside the story of the two lovers.
items.hint3: Three of the options are parts inside the story that the players act out. Ask which option names the one who stands outside the story and speaks to the audience about it.
items.solution:
Answer: D. Prologue

In the workmen's play of Pyramus and Thisby in Act 5, Quince takes the part of the Prologue. A prologue is the opening speech that introduces a play, and in this play-within-a-play the Prologue is treated as a character who comes on to explain the story.

How to tell: Quince tells the audience to 'wonder on, till truth make all things plain' and then introduces each actor: 'This man is Pyramus', 'This beauteous lady Thisby is certain', and so on. Introducing the players and the story is the Prologue's job.

Why not the others:
A. Wall: Wall is played by another workman, the man with lime and rough-cast whom Quince points to.
B. Lion: Lion is played by Snug the joiner, whom Quince introduces later in the same speech.
C. Moonshine: Moonshine is the man with the lantern, dog and bush of thorn, not Quince.

Exam tip: learn the cast of the play-within-a-play as a table: each workman, his trade and his part. Questions on Act 5 often test these links.

items.hint1: When the Prologue ends, the players leave the stage for a moment. Think about who is watching the play and how they react to it.
items.hint2: The next voice is not an actor in the workmen's play. The noble audience comments on the show between the players' speeches.
items.hint3: Narrow to Theseus and Demetrius. They swap a joke about whether the lion will speak: one wonders aloud and the other answers him. Which of them, as host of the wedding feast, would start the comments?
items.solution:
Answer: D. Theseus

During the play of Pyramus and Thisby the nobles watch and make jokes between the actors' speeches. Knowing the order of these comments is part of knowing the plot of Act 5.

How to tell: Quince's Prologue speech ends with the players going off. Theseus then says, 'I wonder if the lion be to speak.' Demetrius replies, 'No wonder, my lord: one lion may, when many asses do.' Only after this does Wall begin his speech.

Why not the others:
A. Demetrius: he speaks second, answering Theseus's joke.
B. Lysander: he comments earlier, after the first part of the Prologue, saying Quince 'hath rid his prologue like a rough colt'.
C. Snout: he speaks next as Wall, but only after Theseus and Demetrius have made their jokes.

Exam tip: for 'who speaks next' questions on the play-within-a-play, remember the pattern: an actor's speech, then comments from the noble audience, then the next actor. Theseus often leads the comments.

items.hint1: Go back to the casting scene in Act 1, where Quince hands out the parts to the workmen, and recall what each man is told to play.
items.hint2: Flute is given the lady's part and complains that he has a beard coming. Starveling is first cast as Thisby's mother, not as a lover.
items.hint3: Narrow to Bottom and Snout. Pyramus is the leading man, the lover who kills himself for love. Which of the two is the eager show-off of the group, keen to play the lover, the tyrant and the lion too?
items.solution:
Answer: A. Bottom

In the workmen's play, Nick Bottom the weaver plays Pyramus, the hero. Quince gives him the part in Act 1 Scene 2, and Bottom, who wants every part, takes it gladly.

How to tell: Quince tells Bottom, 'You can play no part but Pyramus', because Pyramus is 'a sweet-faced man'. It is Bottom who is rehearsing Pyramus in the wood when Puck gives him the ass's head.

Why not the others:
B. Flute: the bellows-mender plays Thisby, Pyramus's lady.
C. Snout: the tinker plays Wall in the performance.
D. Starveling: the tailor plays Moonshine.

Exam tip: learn each workman with his trade and his part, for example Bottom, weaver, Pyramus. Setters mix up the names across options, so a small table in your notes pays off.

items.hint1: Lime and rough-cast are building materials, the kind used to plaster a wall. Recall which workman took the part this man is playing.
items.hint2: Flute plays the lady, and Starveling is the man who carries the lantern.
items.hint3: Narrow to Bottom and Snout. When this character steps forward later in the play, the actor gives his own name in his first lines: 'I, one ___ by name, present a wall'. Which name fits?
items.solution:
Answer: C. Snout

Tom Snout the tinker plays Wall in the workmen's play. The 'lime and rough-cast' are plaster he wears to show he is a wall, and he holds up his fingers to make the chink the lovers whisper through.

How to tell: Quince says this man with lime and rough-cast 'doth present Wall'. When Wall speaks, he introduces himself: 'I, one Snout by name, present a wall.'

Why not the others:
A. Bottom: he plays Pyramus, one of the lovers kept apart by the wall.
B. Flute: he plays Thisby, the other lover.
D. Starveling: he is the man with the lantern, dog and bush of thorn.

Exam tip: in Act 5, each actor is known by his props. Match the prop to the part first, then the part to the workman.

items.hint1: Each man Quince points to is linked to the part he plays. Look at what this man carries and at the word that follows the list of his things.
items.hint2: Lime and rough-cast belong to Wall, and the Prologue is Quince himself, the one doing the introducing.
items.hint3: Narrow to Lion and Moonshine. A lantern gives light at night, and in old stories the man in the moon carries a bundle of thorns and keeps a dog. Which part needs all three?
items.solution:
Answer: B. Moonshine

The workmen fear the audience will not understand their play, so they present even the moonlight as a character. Starveling the tailor plays Moonshine, carrying the man in the moon's lantern, dog and bush of thorn.

How to tell: Quince says 'This man, with lantern, dog and bush of thorn, Presenteth Moonshine'. In old folk belief the man in the moon carried a bundle of thorns and had a dog with him, and the lantern stands for the moon's light.

Why not the others:
A. Lion: Lion is Snug the joiner, who wears a lion's skin and roars, and carries no lantern.
C. Prologue: the Prologue is Quince himself, who is giving this speech.
D. Wall: Wall is the man with lime and rough-cast.

Exam tip: in an extract where one character introduces others, read to the end of each sentence. The answer is often stated in the extract itself, as in 'Presenteth Moonshine'.
